title: SafePool credit sink and temporal quota smoother - PRD draft
content:
Overview
This draft proposes two complementary mechanisms for Dedicated capacity to reduce tail failures during tenant bursts while keeping committed capacity utilization high: a SafePool credit sink (a soft "safety sponge" for short-lived burst excess) and a Temporal Quota Smoother (TQS) that spreads transient load across a configurable window using credit decay. The design focuses on minimizing customer-visible failovers, preserving SLOs for reserved tenants, and providing predictable economics for commit-holders.

Problem statement
- Customers with reserved capacity see occasional short spikes (microbursts) that would either cause preemptions of lower-priority routes or force expensive overprovisioning.
- Hard eviction/strict preemption reduces overall utilization and increases churn/complaints.
- Pure predictive autoscaling is brittle for stochastic workloads (flash promotions, CI workloads, reporting jobs).
- Operators need a lightweight mechanism to absorb bursts without creating noisy neighbors or complicated manual intervention.

Goals
- Reduce immediate hard-failures during microbursts by providing a controlled temporary sink of compute credits.
- Give tenants transparent, measurable burst capacity without permanently increasing committed footprint.
- Avoid long-tail exposure to noisy tenants: any borrowed capacity decays (is reclaimed) on a deterministic schedule.
- Integrate with existing autoscaler signals and routing fallback policies (hot lane -> fallback model variant) with minimal changes.

Non-goals
- This is not a replacement for long-lived capacity provisioning or contractual reserved increases.
- Not intended for continuous, sustained overcommit. Any tenant exceeding threshold duration should be moved to committed capacity or throttled.

Design summary
1) SafePool credit sink: a cross-tenant, per-pool soft buffer implemented as a prioritized credit ledger. When short-term demand exceeds a tenant's reserved headroom, the system will allow best-effort execution funded by SafePool credits. Credits are finite, replenished slowly, and tied to economic permissions (tenants with higher commitment tiers get preferential access).

Key properties:
- Time-bounded: credits have TTLs and an enforced repayment window.
- Metered: token-level accounting for cost transparency; customers see SafePool usage on invoice and console.
- Priority-aware: tiered access (e.g., enterprise > startup > free) and tenant-configured importance flags.

2) Temporal Quota Smoother (TQS): a per-tenant smoothing controller that accepts a burst request and, if the tenant opts in or qualifies, shaves the instantaneous rate by queuing/buffering work over a short horizon (e.g., 30s-5m) using credits to allow slight latency increases instead of rejection.

Key properties:
- Adaptive window length determined by model latency sensitivity and SLOs.
- Guarantees a bounded delay profile — no request will be delayed beyond a configured deadline slice.
- Can operate in two modes: proactive (delay before routing to SafePool) and reactive (use SafePool immediately then smooth repayments).

How components interact
- Normal state: tenant uses reserved capacity and can burst into personal headroom defined in policy.
- Microburst: if headroom exhausted, TQS first attempts to smooth requests if configured. If smoothing cannot absorb the excess (deadline reached) or tenant not enrolled, SafePool credits are consumed.
- Escalation: if SafePool budget exhausted or system-wide pressure crosses thresholds, the standard fallback hierarchy applies (graceful throttling -> model variant fallback -> cross-pool routing to lower-cost region).

Autoscaler integration
- Signal inputs: TQS exposes a short-term "burst pressure" metric to the autoscaler so predictive scaling can factor transient spikes into warm-pool prewarming decisions.
- Learning loop: maintain decay traces of SafePool draws to tune autoscaler thresholds and prewarm heuristics.

Isolation and safety guards
- Per-tenant cap: ceiling on SafePool consumption (absolute and as fraction of reserved tokens).
- Decay and repayment: credits decay back to pool on a schedule and tenants accrue repayment debt that reduces future burst priority until cleared. The repayment curve is configurable per tenant class.
- Silent eviction window: in the rare case of system overload (sustained cluster pressure > X minutes), tenants in SafePool enter a "soft-eviction" grace that shifts their requests to fallback models with explicit notification and billing credits for degraded quality.

Operational playbook (runbook highlights)
- Detection: console alert when SafePool utilization > 60% for > 3m or when many tenants hit per-tenant caps simultaneously.
- Mitigation steps: identify noisy tenants via token-level cost traces, temporarily reduce per-tenant caps, enact regional failover lanes, and communicate via status page if wider impact.
- Customer support: pre-built templated messages for tenants that consumed > 25% of SafePool over 24h; recommend commit increase or application-level rate limiting.

APIs and UX
- Console: new Safety & Burst page showing SafePool usage, per-tenant smoothing configuration, repayment schedule, and hypothetical cost impact.
- API: attach optional burst_policy to Dedicated routes: {"mode":"tqs|sink|hybrid","max_delay_s":30,"burst_priority":10}. (Note: this is a design sketch—final schema TBD.)

Metrics to track
- SafePool utilization %, per-pool and global
- Number of borrow events and average borrow size per tenant
- Missed deadlines under TQS (requests delayed > configured deadline)
- Incidence of soft-evictions and subsequent fallbacks
- Autoscaler warm-pool prewarm rate differences before/after SafePool

Costs & economics
- SafePool usage billed at a premium to discourage abuse (visible on invoice).
- Financial exposure model: compute expected monthly revenue at X% SafePool utilization to bound capital risk.

Rollout plan
1) Internal alpha: enable SafePool in a single region on a small control pool with internal tenants; observe behavior and refine decay curves. 2) Beta with opt-in customers (enterprise customers that explicitly request burst protection). 3) Gradual ramp to GA with default conservative caps and telemetry dashboards.

Open questions / risks
- Pricing friction: will customers accept premium billing for occasional credit use? Need pricing experiments.
- Complexity: interactions between TQS, existing queueing, and autoscaler could create subtle oscillations. Need simulation and stress testing.
- Fairness: designing the priority ladder without hard discrimination is subtle; legal/regulatory considerations for enterprise vs smaller customers.

Next steps & action items (owners)
- Simulate: eng-serving-runtime to build a stochastic workload simulator to model SafePool behavior (owner: Tom).
- API proto: product/API to draft definitive burst_policy schema and console mocks (owner: Priya).
- Economics: finance to run exposure models for 3 utilization scenarios and propose billing tiers (owner: Miguel).
- Runbook: SRE to author detailed incident runbook with concrete threshold numbers (owner: Asha).

Appendix: short simulation sketch
- Use Poisson and Pareto mix workload to surface microburst tails; test TQS windows of 15s/60s/300s; measure reduction in hard evictions and additional latency percentiles.

This is an early design focused on reducing customer-visible failures without major changes to contract mechanics. Feedback welcome—particularly on repayment curves and the product UX for consented burst behavior.
